title: Rethinking the Foundation Subjects
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart describes a pattern he has seen in many primary schools: foundation subjects carry too much content but little clarity about what children should learn. Symptoms include national curriculum statements passed to teachers as an overview, resource-website activities, worksheets that do not make pupils think about the subject, and units that move on regardless of what was learned. His remedy starts by having subject experts specify the exact substantive knowledge, vocabulary, concepts and disciplinary knowledge, and then editing that large body of content down to core knowledge versus hinterland. He argues the sequence of learning should be freed from termly and half-termly boundaries so it takes as long as children need. Because this depends on knowing whether pupils have actually learned, he places formative assessment and responsive teaching at the centre and rejects tracking teacher assessments in these subjects. The unifying question for teachers is what to do when children have not understood, and the curriculum must leave wiggle room to answer it.
points: Planning by the number of weeks available guarantees overstuffing, so the curriculum should be specified in detail first and then deliberately edited down to what is core versus nice to have.
Existing shared drives of slides and tasks need an audit asking what each task makes children think about, so that lovely but weak activities are cut from an already bloated timetable.
A sequence of learning should not be bound by arbitrary term boundaries, because it is a whole-school sequence that takes as long as children need to learn it.
Evidence of learning means recall after time has passed and application in new situations, and formative assessment only matters if time is built in to act on it.
Tracking teacher-assessment grades in foundation subjects adds nothing; the useful move is changing the mindset from lessons to a long-term sequence and a mastery model.
quotes: The trap to avoid is planning by the number of lessons available. It’s tempting. You’d have all that content and only 6-8 weeks (lessons usually) to fit in the most important stuff. But this will always lead to packing in too much.

The national curriculum subject content is not enough to teach from. Subject experts need to specific the exact substantive knowledge that we want children to learn, the associated vocabulary, the concepts that children should develop (and how they’ll develop over time) and the disciplinary knowledge too.

The sequence of learning should not be bound by arbitrary time limits. It will take as long as it takes for children to learn it and this is important because it is part of whole, a sequence of learning that affects the whole school and not just one year group.
Classic conveyor belt education; the next lesson and the next unit of work comes along regardless of what children have learned.

The important question for teachers is: ‘What do you do when children haven’t understood?’ We can’t just move on. We need wiggle room in units of work to spend longer (or shorter) on different ideas so that it is truly responsive to what children know and understand.
No need to track teacher assessments for foundation subjects. We’d simply be putting information into a spreadsheet that then spits out the same information. Pointless.
The importance of assessment in the foundation subjects is that of formative assessment. And formative assessment is only useful if we actually do something with the the information.
